## Assigned Reading

- Title: **Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research**
- Author(s): Sandve G.K., Nekrutenki A., Taylor J., Hovig E.
- Year: 2013
- Journal: PLOS Computational Biology 9(10): e1003285
- <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003285>


## Reflections

::: {.callout-note title="bCourses Submission"}
Submit your answers---to the following questions---to the corresponding 
assignment in bCourses.

Accepted formats: PDF, HTML, MS Word (`.docx`), or Google Doc
:::


### 1. Manual Tweaks

Think of a time you were rushing to meet a project deadline and chose a 
quick manual fix over writing a script.

- Describe a scenario where you used "copy-paste" to format data, or 
manually tweaked a file to make it compatible with a tool. 

- How did bypassing an automated workflow make it harder to catch bugs later? 

- If you had to scale that project to 1,000 files, explain exactly where your 
manual method would completely break down.


### 2. Same script, different outputs

Identify a past project where running the exact same script twice yielded 
slightly different outputs, or where a small change broke everything.

- Detail a case where you failed to set a random seed, leaving you unable to 
duplicate your exact figures. 

- Did you lose a functional version of your script because you were not using 
a version control system like Git? 

- Confess how much time you wasted trying to manually backtrack your code to 
a working state.


### 3. Disconnected Elements

Review a final report or paper you wrote for a previous class. Look at a specific 
chart or data claim you made.

- Where exactly is the raw underlying data for that specific chart stored 
right now? 

- Cite a case where your written conclusions lived in a text document, 
completely disconnected from the server paths or scripts that generated the data. 

- How long would it take a peer to trace your text back to its exact baseline 
numbers?

## Rubric

::: {.callout-important}
Generic responses that do not mention a specific 
past assignment name or unique piece of code from your own experience will 
receive a score of zero.
:::

- **Full Credit (3 Points)**: Response is highly specific, names unique personal 
or localized constraints, and explicitly connects the personal experience 
back to the prompt in each question. Clearly written by a human.

- **Partial Credit (1-2 Points)**: Response is correct but uses vague or generic 
examples (e.g., "I lost a file once" instead of naming the script). Sounds like 
a generic summary an AI could have written.

- **No Credit (0 Points)**: Response relies entirely on abstract definitions, 
fails to provide personal context, or uses copy-pasted text from a webpage
or AI tool.
